In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the human visual system is tuned to faces.
the question whether the face is a special stimulus in visual perception.
the question of how the visual system processes face stimuli and what kind of information processing strategies are involved.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the eye movement patterns are not specific to faces, and the complementary fixation patterns are not specific either.
the face is a special visual object that is processed in a special manner.
eye-tracking is an effective method in the investigation of the mechanisms of face processing and that it provides a new and useful approach to the study of face perception.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the face-specificity of the triangular area is a robust finding, which is independent of inversion and can be observed with a wide range of visual stimuli.
the eye movements of participants are driven not only by the visual features of the face stimuli, but also by a template-driven process, which may reflect a face-specific mechanism.
the eye movements of our participants were influenced by both bottom-up and top-down factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
eye movements during viewing of static, half-faces can be explained by the interplay of stimulus-driven and template-driven processes, and that the latter is likely to be specific to faces.
the triangular region of the face is the most salient part of the face and is fixated first.
the eye-tracking method is a promising tool for the study of face perception, and that it is worth further investigation.
